content.title: About
content.content: Cake made with glutinous rice is a traditional dessert prepared from sticky rice, sugar, coconut milk, and often flavored with vanilla or fruit. The batter becomes soft and slightly sticky, delivering a sweet and delicate taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Glutinous rice is a staple in many Asian cuisines, especially Thai, Vietnamese, and Lao.
The cake is commonly served at celebrations and family gatherings.
Traditionally it is steamed in bamboo baskets, which adds a subtle aroma.
Some regional recipes include matcha green tea or fragrant lemongrass for extra flavor.
Sticky rice contains more amylopectin than regular rice, giving it its characteristic chewiness.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Glutinous rice provides a slow‑release source of energy, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber supports healthy digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1 and B3 aid carbohydrate metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: The cake supplies magnesium and iron, important for muscle function and blood formation.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When prepared without excessive oil, the dessert remains relatively low‑calorie.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Because the cake is sweet, people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: Rare, but an allergic reaction to rice is possible.

items.title: Sticky texture
items.content: The chewiness can be a choking hazard for very young children.

items.title: Gluten considerations
items.content: The cake is naturally gluten‑free, but check added ingredients for hidden gluten.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the cake chilled or slightly warm, cut into bite‑size slices. It pairs well with fruit sauce, coconut cream, or fresh berries. For a lighter version, replace part of the sugar with honey or stevia.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cake in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze it in a sealed bag for up to 2 months. Allow it to come to room temperature before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned fish is fish that has been cooked and sealed in an airtight can. Common varieties include tuna, sardines, salmon, herring, and cod. The canning process preserves most nutrients and gives the product a long shelf life without refrigeration.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canning of fish became widespread in the early 19th century with advances in metalworking and steam boilers.
Tuna in its own juice is one of the most popular canned fish worldwide.
Sardines are often packed in oil, which increases calories but enhances flavor.
Properly sealed cans can keep fish safe to eat for 3–5 years.
In some cuisines canned fish is used in traditional dishes, such as the “California roll” sushi.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Canned fish provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Tuna and sardines are high in EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B12 and B6 in fish help maintain normal nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Canned fish supplies selenium, iodine, and phosphorus, important for thyroid function and bone health.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Almost no carbs make canned fish suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned fish often contains a lot of salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Mercury
items.content: Some fish (e.g., large tuna) may contain mercury; moderate consumption is advised, especially for children and pregnant women.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to seafood may experience reactions to canned fish.

items.title: Bisphenol A (BPA)
items.content: Metal cans can be lined with epoxy resin that may contain BPA; opt for BPA‑free packaging if concerned.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned fish can be eaten straight from the can, added to salads, pastas, sandwiches, or used to make fish cakes. It is common to drain the liquid (water, oil, or brine) and, if desired, rinse the fish before consumption.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer the fish to an airtight container and keep it in the refrigerator, using it within 2–3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Fried salmon is made from salmon fillets that are pan‑ or oven‑fried until a golden crust forms. The cooking method retains most of the beneficial omega‑3 fatty acids while giving the flesh a rich, crispy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Salmon is one of the most valuable commercial fish, harvested in the northern Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
Frying salmon is often accompanied by lemon juice, herbs, and spices to highlight its natural flavor.
A 100 g serving of fried salmon provides over 20 g of high‑quality protein.
Salmon accumulates astaxanthin, a natural carotenoid that gives the flesh its pink hue and antioxidant properties.
In traditional Scandinavian cuisine, salmon is fried in butter for extra richness.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Fried salmon retains EPA and DHA, omega‑3s that support heart and brain health.

items.title: High‑quality protein source
items.content: Salmon protein is easily digested and aids muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin D
items.content: Salmon is one of the few food sources of vitamin D, essential for bones and immunity.

items.title: Contains selenium
items.content: Selenium in salmon contributes to antioxidant defense at the cellular level.

items.title: Supports eye health
items.content: Astaxanthin and vitamin A help maintain healthy vision.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Frying adds cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should consume in moderation.

items.title: Possible contaminants
items.content: Wild salmon may contain mercury and PCBs; choose reputable sources.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish.

items.title: Over‑cooking
items.content: Excessive frying can produce acrylamide, a potentially harmful compound.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve fried salmon hot as a main dish, in salads, with vegetable sides, or in sandwiches. Slice it into strips, drizzle with lemon juice, and garnish with fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked fried salmon in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze it in a bag at –18 °C, where it remains good for up to 2 months.

hot-dog-sandwich-reduced-fat-on-white-br.title: Hot Dog Sandwich, Reduced Fat, on White Bread

content.title: About
content.content: A sandwich featuring a hot‑dog‑style sausage made from lean meat, served between two slices of white bread. The reduced‑fat version uses post‑roasted turkey or chicken meat and minimal oil during cooking. It is popular as a quick snack or light meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The hot dog originated in the United States in the late 19th century and quickly became an iconic street food.
Reduced‑fat versions replace traditional pork sausage with lean turkey or chicken to lower calorie content.
White bread is often lightly toasted to add a crisp texture to the sandwich.
The sandwich is easy to pack in paper wrappers, making it common in food trucks and school cafeterias.
Some regions add a thin slice of cheese to enhance flavor without significantly increasing calories.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The reduced‑fat formulation provides fewer calories from fat, supporting weight‑management diets.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: Lean meat in the sausage supplies high‑quality protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Meat contributes iron, essential for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Carbohydrates for energy
items.content: White bread offers quick‑digesting carbs that supply rapid energy.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both the meat and the bread provide B1, B2, and B6 vitamins that support metabolism.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White bread can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar, which may be problematic for people with diabetes.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Sausages and bread often contain added salt; individuals monitoring sodium should watch portion size.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: White bread contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some pre‑made sausages contain preservatives and nitrites; choose additive‑free options when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich can be enjoyed hot or warm, reheated in a microwave or on a grill. Serve with mustard, ketchup, or a light yogurt‑based sauce. For a more balanced meal, add fresh vegetables such as tomatoes, lettuce, or cucumber.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared sandwich refrigerated at 0–4 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag for up to 1 month. Before eating, heat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C.

rice-brown-with-tomatoes-and-or-tomato-b.title: Brown Rice with Tomatoes and/or Tomato‑Based Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain rice that retains its bran layer and germ. When cooked with tomatoes or a tomato‑based sauce, it gains a rich flavor and an extra boost of vitamins and antioxidants typical of tomatoes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice provides more fiber, B‑vitamins, and minerals than white rice.
Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that becomes more bioavailable after cooking.
Combining whole grains with tomatoes offers longer satiety compared with refined grains alone.
Tomatoes may support cardiovascular health thanks to their potassium and vitamin C content.
In many cultures, rice with tomato sauce is a traditional festive dish.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: The fiber in brown rice supports healthy digestion and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs provide a steady release of energy, beneficial for active individuals.

items.title: Lycopene and tomato antioxidants
items.content: Lycopene protects cells from oxidative stress and may lower the risk of certain chronic diseases.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Tomatoes add vitamin C, vitamin K, potassium, and folate, while brown rice contributes magnesium and iron.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: The combination of fiber, potassium, and antioxidants can help reduce blood pressure and cholesterol levels.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Brown rice contains phytic acid, which can inhibit the absorption of some minerals if consumed in excess.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes.

items.title: High glycemic index when over‑processed
items.content: Over‑cooking the rice or adding sugar to the sauce can raise the dish’s glycemic index.

items.title: Sodium in prepared sauces
items.content: Commercial tomato sauces often contain added salt; monitor the amount used.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve cooked brown rice with a tomato sauce, fresh diced tomatoes, or tomato purée. Enhance with herbs (basil, oregano), a drizzle of olive oil, or a sprinkle of Parmesan cheese. It works well as a side for meat, fish, or vegetarian dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry brown rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked rice with tomato sauce should be kept in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat thoroughly before serving.
